title: The Day Is Near
sum: Zephaniah opens with the LORD announcing an end: everything off the surface of the ground, people and animals, birds and fish. Then the aim narrows to Judah and Jerusalem. The LORD names who will go: the last of Baal's worship, the idol priests, the people who bow to the stars on their roofs and swear by the LORD and by Milcom in one breath, and those who never sought him at all.

A hush falls (1:7), because the day of the LORD is a sacrifice with invited guests. The officials, the merchants and the comfortable men who think the LORD does nothing are searched out with lamps. The chapter ends with the great day itself, built in short, hammering lines: a day of fury, darkness, the ram's horn and the battle cry. Silver and gold cannot buy anyone out.
readings: Read as the coming Babylonian conquest

A warning to the Judah of Josiah's early years. The "day" arrives in 597 and 586 BC when Babylon takes Jerusalem; the "guests" are the army (Isaiah 13:3; Jeremiah 6:4). The sweeping words of 1:2-3 are the language of total disaster, as in Jeremiah 4:23-26.
Read as the end of the age

The words "the whole earth" and "everyone who lives on the earth" (1:18) point beyond Judah. Jewish and Christian readers since antiquity have heard in 1:14-18 the last day, and the Latin church made 1:15 the opening of its hymn for the dead.

Short lines, piled images and repeated sounds (a day of... a day of...) make the chapter a poem meant to be heard and to shock. Its details (the Mortar, the Second District) are named so that every hearer sees his own street.

views.H: The chapter belongs to the reign of Josiah (640-609 BC), almost certainly before the reform of 622, because Baal's worship, idol priests, rooftop star-worship and Milcom are still there (1:4-5). The "king's sons" (1:8) suggests the royal house in the boyhood of a king. The invader the prophet has in mind is most likely Babylon, though Babylon is not named; Jeremiah's "foe from the north" (Jeremiah 1:13-15) is the nearest parallel. The older view that Scythian horsemen (Herodotus, Histories 1.103-106) were the foe has few defenders now.
views.C: The heading (1:1) is the only prose; the rest is poetry. Many critics see 1:2-3 and 1:18 as a frame, and some think 1:2-3 were added; others (Berlin, Sweeney) read the chapter as a unit from Josiah's time. The Greek text differs in several places (1:3, 1:4, 1:9, 1:10), showing that the Hebrew text was already being read and revised. The book belongs to the "day of the LORD" tradition, which Amos 5:18-20 starts and Zephaniah gathers (von Rad, Mowinckel).
views.J: The Hebrew Bible counts Zephaniah within the one scroll of the Twelve (Bava Batra 14b-15a). The Talmud cites 1:12, "I will search Jerusalem with lamps," in discussing why the search for leaven before Passover uses a lamp (Bavli Pesachim 7b-8a). This lens is thin here: no Targum or medieval commentator is quoted.
views.X: The Latin church read 1:15-16 as the last judgment: Jerome's Vulgate has "dies irae, dies illa," which opens the Dies irae. Jerome, who made the Vulgate, also wrote a commentary on Zephaniah (about AD 393). Christian readers have tied Zephaniah's day both to the fall of Jerusalem and to the judgment at Christ's return. 2 Peter 3:7-12 describes the day of the Lord with fire in language close to 1:18.
views.F: Futurist readers take 1:2-3 and 1:14-18 as pictures of the end of the age. Dispensationalists place "the day of the LORD" in the tribulation and the reign of Christ that follows; amillennial and postmillennial readers see it as the final judgment at Christ's return; preterist readers see it fulfilled in 586 BC and, for the Gospels, in AD 70. The language of fire consuming the whole earth (1:18; 3:8) is the closest Old Testament match to 2 Peter 3:10.

deep.b: The heading dates the book to Josiah's reign. The usual picture: Josiah came to the throne at eight in 640 BC; at sixteen he began to seek God; at twenty he started to purge Judah (2 Chronicles 34:3); at twenty-six, in 622 BC, the law-book was found and the great reform followed (2 Kings 22-23). Zephaniah's list of sins (Baal's remnant, the idol priests, roof worship, Milcom, foreign dress) looks like what Josiah was about to remove, so most scholars place the prophecy between 640 and 622. A few place it later in the reign or after Josiah's death in 609. A group of critics think much of the book is later and was shaped after the exile. The Plain does not decide: it shows the evidence in the notes.

deep.h: The Scythians: a theory and its problems
deep.b: The Greek historian Herodotus tells how nomad Scythians swept through western Asia for twenty-eight years, defeated the Medes, and reached the border of Egypt, plundering the temple of the goddess at Ashkelon (Histories 1.103-106). In the 1800s and early 1900s many scholars thought Zephaniah's invader, and Jeremiah's "foe from the north," was this Scythian raid. The theory is attractive, but Zephaniah never names an invader, the Babylonian records do not mention a Scythian invasion of Judah, and Herodotus's account is the only source. Most recent commentators think the foe was Babylon, or that Zephaniah did not name the foe on purpose. The theory is a view, not a fact.

Genesis 1 builds the world in an order: sea creatures and birds, then land animals and people. Zephaniah 1:2-3 lists the victims in reverse. The flood story speaks of wiping out life from the surface of the ground (Genesis 6:7; 7:4); Zephaniah repeats that wording. Jeremiah 4:23-26 does the same with "shapeless and empty" (Genesis 1:2). Together these show that the prophets thought of judgment as creation undone. The same prophets promise a new start, which in Zephaniah comes in 3:9-20 as pure lips, a humble people and God's own joy.

deep.title: One idea in three names: the sweep that is also a harvest
deep.b: The first verb of the book, 'asaf, can mean "gather in" as well as "sweep away." The prophets use it for both: a harvest (Jeremiah 8:13) and a gathering of survivors (Micah 2:12). My suggestion is that Zephaniah's first words are meant to sound like a harvest that turns out to be a catastrophe, and that the book's last chapter turns the same verb around (3:8, 3:18-20). I have not seen this argued exactly this way. It rests on 1:2-3, 3:8 and 3:18-20, and it overlaps with commentators who note the pun in 1:2.

echoes: Genesis 6:7; Genesis 7:4; Jeremiah 4:23-26; Hosea 4:3; Amos 5:18-20; Isaiah 13:6-13; Joel 1:15; Joel 2:1-2; Habakkuk 2:20; Deuteronomy 28:28-30; 2 Kings 22-23; 2 Peter 3:7-12; Revelation 6:12-17

settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, hearing the prophet in the capital
settings.when: In the reign of Josiah (640 to 609 BC), most likely before the reform of 622
settings.why: To make a people who think the LORD "does nothing" (1:12) face a judge who acts, by opening with a verdict that is wider than Judah and then closing in on it. Knowing it is a spoken warning to people who thought themselves safe changes the sweep of "everything" from a forecast of the end to a shock at the start of a sermon.
views: The words are meant literally: a universal judgment, as in the flood or at the end of the age (the plain reading, and that of many Christian readers).
The sweeping words describe a disaster on Judah, as Jeremiah 4:23-26 does of a land laid waste (the usual critical reading).

settings.what: Charges against Jerusalem's idolaters, officials and merchants
settings.to: The rulers, priests, merchants and settled householders of Jerusalem
settings.when: In Josiah's early or middle years, before the Temple reform (1:4-5 shows the shrines still standing)
settings.why: To name the sins that mark the people of a covenant that has gone cold: worship of other powers beside the LORD, a court in foreign clothes, violence and fraud, a market that deals in silver, and the comfortable who think God will do nothing. Naming streets and gates (the Fish Gate, the Second District, the Mortar) makes each hearer see his own place on the list.
settings.readers: For later readers, including the exiles who kept the book, the list explained why the day had come.
views: The commonest view: the cult of Baal and the host of heaven are still in place (Berlin, Sweeney).
Some place the oracles after 622, when "the remnant of Baal" (1:4) means what the reform had not yet reached.

settings.what: The great day of the LORD
settings.to: The people of Judah, in the same sermon
settings.when: In Josiah's reign, as a warning of a day that is already "near"
settings.why: To strip away the hope that the day of the LORD will be a victory for his people (compare Amos 5:18-20), and to tell them that their silver and gold, the safety they trust in, will not buy a way out. Knowing it was spoken to those who expected the day to favor them explains why its imagery is all darkness.
settings.readers: Later readers in exile and under foreign rule heard it as the explanation of what had happened and as a call to the humble to seek the LORD (2:3).
views: The day is a historical event: 597 and 586 BC.
The day is the end of the age, and the book reads past Judah to the whole earth.

traditions.q: What is "the day of the LORD" in Zephaniah 1:14-18, and is it still to come? (The confessions below agree on a final judgment; readings differ on whether Zephaniah's day is also a near, historical one: see the Futurist view above.)
views: The day of the LORD, like the prophets' other warnings, looks to the Last Judgment at Christ's return, when the secrets of hearts are revealed (Catechism 1038-1041). The Latin of 1:15 gave the Church the hymn Dies irae.

The church confesses in the Creed that Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead. The prophets' day is read as a call to repent and is remembered each year on the Sunday of the Last Judgment before Lent.
At the end of the world Christ will appear for judgment and raise all the dead, giving the godly eternal life and condemning the ungodly (Augsburg Confession, Article 17).
God has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by Christ (Westminster Confession 33).
God has appointed a day in which he will judge the world by Jesus Christ (Second London Confession, chapter 32).

"The day of the LORD" is a future period that begins with the judgments of the tribulation and ends in the reign of Christ; Zephaniah 1 and 3 describe both its terror and its blessing (Scofield Reference Bible notes on the day of the Lord).

title: Seek the LORD, Then the Nations
sum: After the roar of chapter 1, a quiet call: gather yourselves, seek the LORD, you humble of the land, seek righteousness, seek humility. "Perhaps you will be hidden on the day of the LORD's anger." The word is "perhaps"; the prophet will not promise what God has not promised.

Then the map turns. The prophet sweeps around the compass. West, the Philistine cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron, will be emptied and their coast given to the remnant of Judah. East, Moab and Ammon, who mocked God's people, will become like Sodom and Gomorrah. South, the Cushites will fall by the LORD's sword. North, Assyria and its proud capital Nineveh, who said "I am, and besides me there is nothing," will become a lair for owls and hedgehogs.
readings: A set of oracles against Judah's neighbors in the years when Assyria was failing and Babylon was rising. Ashkelon fell in 604, Nineveh in 612, and the Philistine cities lost their independence. Moab and Ammon were later ravaged.
Read as a map of the world
One nation at each point of the compass stands for all the nations. The LORD's judgment reaches everywhere, and so does his later call (2:11): all the coastlands bow to him.
Read as a warning to Judah
The oracles are told to Judah, not to the nations. The point for hearers in Jerusalem is that a God who judges Nineveh judges Jerusalem too (3:1), and that the humble who seek him are safe.

views.H: The Philistine cities (2:4-7) suffered from Egypt (Ashdod's long siege, Gaza taken by Pharaoh) and then from Babylon (Ashkelon destroyed in 604 BC). Nineveh fell in 612 to Babylonians and Medes, ending the Assyrian empire (2 Kings 23:29; Nahum). Moab and Ammon were attacked by Babylon (Jeremiah 48-49; Josephus, Antiquities 10.9.7). If Zephaniah spoke in Josiah's early years, the Assyrian oracle is a bold prophecy against the world power of the day.
views.C: Critics ask whether the Moab and Ammon oracle (2:8-11), with its references to the remnant of Judah and to the gods of the earth, belongs to Josiah's time or is later (Ben Zvi). The prose style, the "I" and "he" of 2:12-13, and the Hebrew puns of 2:4 are also discussed. The text is hard in 2:1-2, 2:6 and 2:14, and the Greek differs at 2:1, 2:2, 2:6, 2:9 (Damascus), 2:14.
views.J: The Jewish canon counts the Twelve as one scroll (Bava Batra 14b-15a), so Nahum, which is about the fall of Nineveh, and Jonah, which is about its repentance, sit in the same scroll as Zephaniah. No rabbinic passage on these oracles is quoted here.
views.X: Christian readers have found in 2:11 the worship of the whole world, and in the humble of 2:3 the first picture of those blessed in Matthew 5:3-5. The church's reading of 2:11 as the conversion of the nations to Christ is a later application, not the prophet's words.
views.F: Futurist readers take 2:11 ("all the coastlands of the nations" bowing down) as a picture of the world after the final judgment, and some see Moab, Ammon, Cush and Assyria as names for the peoples of the end time. Others see them as past events only.

deep.b: Chapter 2 names a people at each point of the compass: the Philistines in the west (the sea coast), Moab and Ammon in the east, Cush in the south and Assyria in the north. Many commentators see the pattern as deliberate, a way of saying that the LORD's reach covers every direction. Amos 1-2 uses the same device, a ring of oracles on the nations around Israel and Judah. Judah sits in the middle, and in 3:1 the prophet turns inward to Jerusalem, which has been under judgment all along.

Zephaniah's Nineveh is a proud city that says "I am, and besides me there is nothing." Nahum's is a city of blood and lies (Nahum 3:1). Jonah's is a city that repents at five words and is spared (Jonah 3). All three books are in the Twelve, and they do not agree on Nineveh's character, but each shows the same city at a different time. Reading them in order shows God's mercy offered, then withdrawn after a later generation went back to violence.

echoes: Amos 1-2; Isaiah 13-23; Jeremiah 46-51; Ezekiel 25-32; Genesis 19:24-38; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 11:14; Isaiah 34:11-15; Isaiah 47:8-10; Nahum 2-3; Jonah 3; Genesis 10:5

settings.what: A call to the humble to seek the LORD
settings.to: Usually taken to be Judah (the "nation without shame"; the Greek reads "untaught nation," and the variant gives the other readings), and within it the humble of the land
settings.when: In Josiah's reign, before the day arrives
settings.why: To offer a way out to those who will take it: gather, seek, do justice, be humble, and perhaps be hidden. It also sets the humble apart from the proud for the rest of the book. Hearing it as a call to a people who were told in chapter 1 that nothing can save them makes the "perhaps" an opening, not a threat.
views: A call to Judah as a whole
The "nation" is Judah, whose shame has run out (Berlin).
A call to the faithful few
The humble of the land are a group inside the nation who are told to keep seeking (the anawim, Gelin).

settings.what: The word against the Philistine cities
settings.to: Judah, hearing of her old enemies on the western coast
settings.when: In Josiah's reign, when the Philistine cities lay between Egypt and Babylon
settings.why: To tell Judah that the old neighbors who had raided and ruled her will be emptied, and her remnant will graze their land. It teaches Judah that the LORD owns the map.
settings.readers: Later readers, after Babylon destroyed Ashkelon (604 BC) and Judah lost its own land, heard it as a promise that the coast would be given back.

settings.what: The word against Moab and Ammon
settings.to: Judah, hearing of Moab and Ammon, kin who mocked her
settings.when: Debated: in Josiah's reign, or later after Judah's fall
settings.why: To answer insults against God's people with an oath: they will share Sodom's end, and the survivors of Judah will take their land. It also looks past it to the nations bowing to the LORD from their own places (2:11).
views: Moab and Ammon had long mocked Judah (a common reading).
The insults fit the fall of Judah, so the passage may be later (Ben Zvi and others).

settings.by: The LORD, in the first person ("my sword")
settings.to: Judah, hearing of the far south
settings.when: In Josiah's reign, when Egypt under the Saite kings was Judah's neighbor and Cush was its distant memory
settings.why: To complete the compass with the south: no part of the world escapes. It is one line, the shortest oracle in the book.

settings.what: The word against Assyria and Nineveh
settings.when: Probably in Josiah's early years, while Assyria still ruled; Nineveh fell in 612 BC
settings.why: To tell a people who had paid tribute to Assyria for a century that the empire, which said "I am, and besides me there is nothing," would end as a home for owls. Knowing Judah had lived under that empire explains the vividness of the ruin scene.
settings.readers: After 612 BC the oracle was read as fulfilled, with Nahum.

title: Pure Lips and a Rejoicing God
sum: Back to Jerusalem. "Woe to the rebellious and defiled city." She has listened to no voice, taken no correction, trusted no one and come near to no one. Her officials are lions, her judges are wolves at dusk, her prophets are reckless, and her priests treat the holy as common. Yet the LORD in her midst does no wrong: every morning he brings his justice to light. The nations he cut off did not teach her, and her people got up early to corrupt everything they did.

Then the turn. "Wait for me": he will gather the nations to pour out his anger, and the whole earth will burn. And then: "I will change the lips of the peoples into pure lips," so that all call on the LORD's name. He leaves behind a humble, afflicted people who do no wrong. The book ends in a shout of joy: Daughter Zion, give a ringing cry! The warrior who rescues is in your midst, quiet in his love, cheering over you with a ringing shout. He gathers the lame and the outcast and turns their shame to praise.
readings: Read as a promise to the exiles
If the last part was written or added in the exile, 3:14-20 is God's word to a scattered people: I will bring you in, gather you, turn your fortunes around.
Read as the ending of Josiah-era preaching
In the Josiah-era reading, the last section is a hope held out to the humble in Jerusalem, with the nations' conversion as the horizon.
Christian readers hear in 3:9 the gift of tongues at Pentecost, in 3:12 the Beatitudes and in 3:14-17 the greeting of Gabriel to Mary.

views.H: In Josiah's time Jerusalem's leaders were exactly what 3:3-4 describes, and Jeremiah's preaching in the same years paints the same picture (Jeremiah 5; 7; 23). The reform of 622 was real, and a prophet might have said that it had not touched the heart (compare Jeremiah 3:10). If 3:14-20 is from Zephaniah's time, it is a hope for the humble; if later, a word to exiles. The promise of return fits the 500s BC well.
views.C: The ending (3:9-20, or at least 3:14-20) is the most disputed part. Many critics date some or all of it to the exile or later: the language of gathering the scattered and turning fortunes around fits a post-586 world. Defenders of the book's unity point out that hope after judgment is part of the prophets' pattern, and that the "remnant" language of 2:7 and 3:12-13 is already in the earlier chapters. The Hebrew of 3:10, 3:17 and 3:18 is hard, and the Greek differs in each. The scroll Mur88 (early 100s AD) preserves much of chapter 3 in the same consonants as the Masoretic Text, including 3:17 and 3:18.
views.J: Jewish readers have set 3:14-20 beside the other promises of return in the Twelve, which sit in one scroll (Bava Batra 14b-15a). No rabbinic or medieval passage on chapter 3 is quoted here, and Jewish readings of "pure lips" (3:9) are not documented.
views.X: The church heard 3:9 with Pentecost (Acts 2), 3:10 with the Ethiopian official of Acts 8, 3:12 with the Beatitudes, 3:14-17 with the Annunciation (Luke 1:28-33) and 3:16 with John 12:15. Jerome's Latin of 3:8, "the day of my resurrection," led Christian commentators to connect it to Christ's rising. These are the church's readings of the Greek and Latin text and are labeled as such in the notes.
views.F: Futurist readers take 3:9-20 as the world after the final judgment: the nations purified, the scattered gathered, Zion rejoicing. Dispensationalist readers set this in the millennial kingdom; amillennial readers set it in the church and the new creation; Jewish readers set it in the age to come. The verse that closes the book, 3:20, is open to all of these.

deep.b: One Hebrew word, qerev, "inside, midst," runs through chapter 3. Her officials are lions "in her midst" (3:3). The LORD is righteous "in her midst" (3:5). He removes the proud "from your midst" (3:11) and leaves the afflicted "in your midst" (3:12). Finally the LORD, Israel's King, is "in your midst" (3:15) and again (3:17). The chapter asks who stands at the center of the city. By the end, the answer is the LORD, and the center has been cleared of lions, wolves and the proud.
deep.refs: Zephaniah 3:3; Zephaniah 3:5; Zephaniah 3:11; Zephaniah 3:12; Zephaniah 3:15; Zephaniah 3:17

deep.b: The book's last chapter turns around several sounds from the first. The "battle cry" (teru'ah) of 1:16 becomes Israel's shout of joy (3:14). The "warrior" (gibbor) who cried out in 1:14 is the warrior who rescues in 3:17. The "gathering" ('asaf) that began as an ending in 1:2 is the gathering of the lame and outcast in 3:18-20. The "shame" (bosheth) that the wrongdoer lacks in 3:5 is the shame God takes away and turns into praise in 3:19-20. Reading the book as a whole means hearing the sounds a second time.
deep.refs: Zephaniah 1:2; Zephaniah 1:14; Zephaniah 1:16; Zephaniah 3:5; Zephaniah 3:14; Zephaniah 3:17; Zephaniah 3:19

deep.h: Pure lips: Babel, Isaiah and Pentecost
deep.b: "Lip" is the Hebrew word for language. At Babel the LORD confused the lips of the earth (Genesis 11:7-9). In Isaiah's vision the prophet says he is a man of unclean lips and a coal cleans them (Isaiah 6:5-7). Zephaniah 3:9 promises the peoples "pure lips," and the reader may hear all three: cleansed speech (Isaiah), one speech again (Babel reversed) and the many languages of Pentecost. The next clause ("so that all call on the name of the LORD") makes the purpose clear: it is not a language lesson but an act of worship.

echoes: Jeremiah 5; Jeremiah 7:28; Ezekiel 22:23-31; Habakkuk 1:8; Genesis 11:1-9; Joel 2:32; Acts 2:1-21; Romans 10:13; Isaiah 18:1; Isaiah 6:5-7; Matthew 5:3-5; Luke 6:20; Zechariah 9:9; John 12:15; Luke 1:28-33; Deuteronomy 26:19; Lamentations 1:4

settings.to: Jerusalem: its officials, judges, prophets and priests
settings.when: In Josiah's reign, after the oracles on the nations
settings.why: To turn the whole sermon on those who listened to it. After hearing God judge the nations, Jerusalem is told it is no better: no one listened, no one learned. The list of leaders is a list of those who should have taught her.
views: The city is Jerusalem (nearly all commentators).

settings.what: Wait for me: the nations purified and a humble remnant
settings.to: The faithful of Jerusalem, told to wait; behind them, the nations
settings.when: The point is placed at "the day I rise up"; the date of the writing is debated (Josiah's time, or the exile)
settings.why: To tell the faithful what to do while the judgment falls: wait for God, because after the judgment he will make the peoples worship him with pure lips and leave behind a humble, truthful people. Knowing the first hearers were people who had been told nothing could save them makes the promise of a remnant stand out.
settings.readers: For exiles or the post-exilic community, the promise was a reason to keep on trusting the LORD.
views: The promise was part of the original oracle (Sweeney, who reads the book as a Josianic unit).
The turn to the nations and the remnant belongs to a later hand (many critics).

settings.what: The shout of joy of Daughter Zion
settings.by: The prophet, calling Zion to shout for joy; then the LORD speaks (3:18-20)
settings.to: Zion, Jerusalem and Israel, as a personified daughter
settings.when: Debated: Josiah's time, or after the fall of Jerusalem
settings.why: To end the book not with the day of the LORD but with the LORD's joy: a warrior who rescues, a king in her midst, a God who cries out for joy over her and gathers the lame and the outcast. Knowing it follows chapters of judgment makes the joy the answer to them, not a change of subject.
settings.readers: Exiles and later worshipers read it as the promise to return, and the church as the promise of Christ's coming among his people.
views: A real promise, with 3:18-20 as the hardest verses to date.
Language of gathering the scattered fits after 586 (many critics).

traditions.q: Will people of every nation call on the LORD's name and be saved (3:9)?
views: Those who through no fault of their own do not know Christ's gospel but seek God and try to do his will may achieve salvation (Lumen Gentium 16). Separately, Nostra Aetate 4 cites Zephaniah 3:9 in a sentence about the Church awaiting the day when all peoples call on the Lord with one voice and serve him together; the document does not tie that sentence to the question of who is saved.
People who do not profess the Christian religion cannot be saved, however diligently they live by the light of nature (Westminster Confession 10.4). The confession does not discuss Zephaniah 3:9.

The Second London Confession, chapter 10, paragraph 4, takes the same view as the Westminster Confession: those who do not profess the Christian religion cannot be saved. It does not discuss Zephaniah 3:9.

The Church holds that salvation is in Christ and in his Church, and Orthodox teachers (Kallistos Ware in The Orthodox Church) decline to say where the Church is not, leaving the fate of those outside to God's mercy.

traditions.q: Is the echo of Zephaniah 3:14-17 in Luke 1:28-33 about Mary, or about Christ coming to Zion?
views: Lumen Gentium 55 calls Mary the "exalted Daughter of Sion" but does not cite Zephaniah; its footnotes cite Genesis 3:15, Isaiah 7:14, Micah 5:2-3 and Matthew 1:22-23. The link to Zephaniah is made by the lectionary, which reads Zephaniah 3:14-18 at the Visitation (31 May) and on the Third Sunday of Advent in Year C, and by Catholic readers who hear Gabriel's "Rejoice" (Luke 1:28) in the Greek of Zephaniah 3:14.
No Orthodox source on this echo is cited here.
Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Article 21, answers a different question, whether the saints should be invoked, and rejects invocation as a commanded practice. It does not discuss Zephaniah.
No Reformed source on this echo is cited here.
No Baptist source on this echo is cited here.
